name: syntactic_constructions
description: Clause- and sentence-level machinery of English prose: absolutes, participial and appositive modifiers, sentence architectures, coordination and subordination, focus and information-packaging constructions, ellipsis, interruption, modifier placement, and length moves.

absolute_constructions.name: nominative absolute
absolute_constructions.definition: A noun phrase plus a participle (or other predicative complement) attached to a main clause without a conjunction or a relative pronoun, grammatically independent of it but semantically bound to it.
absolute_constructions.example: Her hands still shaking, she signed the settlement where the lawyer pointed.
absolute_constructions.effect: Layers a second, simultaneous fact onto the main action without demoting it to a full subordinate clause; adds texture at low grammatical cost.
absolute_constructions.register: neutral to literary; common in fiction, narrative nonfiction, and formal exposition, rare in speech
absolute_constructions.caution: Two or three per page reads as craft; two per paragraph reads as a tic.

absolute_constructions.name: present-participial absolute
absolute_constructions.definition: A nominative absolute whose participle is the -ing form, giving the attached circumstance ongoing or simultaneous aspect.
absolute_constructions.example: The generators humming behind the tent, the surgeons worked past midnight.
absolute_constructions.effect: Holds a background process in view for the duration of the main clause.

absolute_constructions.name: past-participial absolute
absolute_constructions.definition: A nominative absolute whose participle is the -ed/-en form, so the attached circumstance is completed before or at the moment of the main clause.
absolute_constructions.example: The contracts signed, the lawyers went to lunch.
absolute_constructions.effect: Compresses a whole prior event into a phrase, producing brisk sequence without 'after' or 'once'.
absolute_constructions.caution: Overuse produces a clipped, faintly military cadence.

absolute_constructions.name: verbless absolute
absolute_constructions.definition: An absolute with no participle at all — a noun phrase followed by a bare predicative noun or adjective, the copula understood.
absolute_constructions.example: His face a mask, he read the verdict aloud.
absolute_constructions.effect: Maximum compression: an image is asserted without a verb to slow it.
absolute_constructions.caution: Reads as mannered in plain expository prose.

absolute_constructions.name: adjectival absolute
absolute_constructions.definition: An absolute whose predicate is an adjective phrase, often extended by a prepositional complement.
absolute_constructions.example: The road slick with rain, we took the long way around the ridge.
absolute_constructions.effect: Supplies the condition under which the main clause happens, in the form of an image rather than a because-clause.

absolute_constructions.name: prepositional absolute
absolute_constructions.definition: An absolute whose predicate is a prepositional phrase locating or situating the noun.
absolute_constructions.example: The children already at the table, we sat down without ceremony.
absolute_constructions.effect: Sets a spatial or temporal stage cheaply, before the main clause claims attention.

absolute_constructions.name: with-absolute
absolute_constructions.definition: An absolute introduced by the preposition 'with' (or occasionally 'without'), which licenses the construction in registers where the bare absolute would sound stiff.
absolute_constructions.example: With the roof gone, the rain came straight down onto the ledgers.
absolute_constructions.effect: Softens the absolute toward ordinary speech; makes the attached circumstance feel causal or enabling.
absolute_constructions.register: neutral; the everyday English realization of the absolute

absolute_constructions.name: without-absolute
absolute_constructions.definition: The negative augmented absolute: 'without' plus a noun phrase and predicate, asserting the absence of the attached circumstance.
absolute_constructions.example: Without a single lamp burning in the street, the town looked abandoned.
absolute_constructions.effect: States a missing condition as vividly as a present one — negation with an image attached.

absolute_constructions.name: what-with absolute
absolute_constructions.definition: A colloquial causal absolute headed by 'what with', typically listing two or more contributing circumstances.
absolute_constructions.example: What with the strike and the snow, nothing left the depot for nine days.
absolute_constructions.effect: Gives a folksy, spoken causality — a shrug where 'because' would be an argument.
absolute_constructions.register: informal; useful for voice in first-person narration and columns

absolute_constructions.name: there-being absolute
absolute_constructions.definition: An absolute built on existential 'there' plus 'being', usually stating that some condition does or does not obtain.
absolute_constructions.example: There being no objection, the chair moved to the next item.
absolute_constructions.effect: Formal, procedural compression of a whole enabling condition.
absolute_constructions.caution: Anywhere but institutional prose it sounds like a minute-taker wrote it.

absolute_constructions.name: fronted absolute
absolute_constructions.definition: An absolute placed before the main clause, so the attached circumstance is read as the frame for what follows.
absolute_constructions.example: The tide already turning, the crew hauled the last crate up the beach.
absolute_constructions.effect: Sets conditions first; the main clause lands inside a scene that is already running.

absolute_constructions.name: trailing absolute
absolute_constructions.definition: An absolute placed after the main clause, adding a detail that the clause has just made relevant.
absolute_constructions.example: She stepped out of the courtroom, her coat over one arm, the reporters already moving.
absolute_constructions.effect: Extends the sentence past its grammatical completion, the way the eye keeps taking in detail after the event.
absolute_constructions.register: literary; a signature of the cumulative style

absolute_constructions.name: medial absolute
absolute_constructions.definition: An absolute wedged between the subject and predicate of the main clause, held off by commas.
absolute_constructions.example: The witness, his hands flat on the rail, said nothing for a long moment.
absolute_constructions.effect: Delays the verb and so enacts the pause it describes.
absolute_constructions.caution: Heavy medial insertions strand the reader between subject and verb; keep them short.

absolute_constructions.name: stacked absolutes
absolute_constructions.definition: Two or more absolutes in series attached to a single main clause.
absolute_constructions.example: He waited at the gate, his ticket folded twice, his bag between his feet, the platform emptying behind him.
absolute_constructions.effect: Builds an accumulating still life; the base clause stops while detail keeps arriving.
absolute_constructions.caution: Past three, the sentence stops feeling observed and starts feeling inventoried.

absolute_constructions.name: absolute with pronoun subject
absolute_constructions.definition: An absolute whose noun phrase is a personal pronoun, which in English keeps subjective case ('he', not 'him') in careful prose.
absolute_constructions.example: She having already refused twice, the committee stopped asking.
absolute_constructions.effect: Marks the absolute as consciously formal; the case choice is itself a register signal.
absolute_constructions.caution: 'Him having refused' is common in speech and will read as an error in print.

absolute_constructions.name: ablative absolute
absolute_constructions.definition: The Latin construction — a noun and participle in the ablative case, syntactically detached from the main clause — from which the English absolute descends; the ancestor of most absolute patterns in formal English.
absolute_constructions.example: Latin 'signo dato, naves solverunt' becomes, in the closest English, 'The signal given, the ships cast off.'
absolute_constructions.effect: Compresses a subordinate event into two or three words, leaving the main clause unencumbered — the reason translators reach for it and the reason English absolutes still feel Latinate.
absolute_constructions.register: the English descendants range from formal to literary; the calque itself is a translator's move
renderings: nominative absolute: 'The signal given, the ships cast off.'
past-participial absolute: 'The orders received, the legion broke camp.'
with-absolute: 'With the signal given, the ships cast off.'
temporal clause: 'When the signal had been given, the ships cast off.'
causal clause: 'Because the signal had been given, the ships cast off.'
concessive clause: 'Although the signal had been given, the ships stayed.'
conditional clause: 'If the signal is given, the ships cast off.'
prepositional phrase: 'At the signal, the ships cast off.'
coordinated clause: 'The signal was given and the ships cast off.'
perfect participial phrase: 'Having received the signal, the crews cast off.'
absolute_constructions.caution: A translated absolute keeps Latin's word order and can leave the English participle dangling; check that the absolute's noun is not mistaken for the main clause's subject.

absolute_constructions.name: genitive absolute
absolute_constructions.definition: The Greek counterpart of the ablative absolute: a noun and participle in the genitive, detached from the main clause; it reaches English chiefly through biblical and classical translation.
absolute_constructions.example: 'These things having been said, he went out' preserves the Greek shape; idiomatic English prefers 'When he had said this, he went out.'
absolute_constructions.effect: In translation it produces the archaic, scriptural cadence readers associate with the King James register.
absolute_constructions.register: translation English; archaic or deliberately liturgical
renderings: perfect participial phrase: 'Having said these things, he went out.'
nominative absolute: 'These things said, he went out.'
temporal clause: 'When he had said these things, he went out.'
sequential coordination: 'He said these things and went out.'
prepositional phrase: 'After that, he went out.'
absolute_constructions.caution: Word-for-word rendering yields the 'and it came to pass' texture — powerful once, wearying twice.

absolute_constructions.name: accusative absolute
absolute_constructions.definition: A minor classical absolute (Greek, with impersonal participles; occasional in late Latin) in the accusative case, typically expressing a granted or permitted circumstance.
absolute_constructions.example: The impersonal 'it being permitted' preserves its shape: 'It being permitted, the delegation entered.'
absolute_constructions.effect: Reads as an official concession or granted condition rather than an observed one.
renderings: impersonal absolute: 'It being permitted, they entered.'
there-being absolute: 'There being no impediment, they entered.'
concessive clause: 'Since it was permitted, they entered.'

absolute_constructions.name: dangling absolute
absolute_constructions.definition: An absolute whose implied subject is left so vague that readers attach it to the main clause's subject and produce a false reading.
absolute_constructions.example: Faulty: 'Driving north, the mileage improved.' Repaired: 'Driving north, we watched the mileage improve.'
absolute_constructions.effect: Named here as the failure mode of the pattern: the absolute's whole advantage is that it carries its own subject, and the error is to omit it.
absolute_constructions.caution: Test every absolute by asking whose action it names; if the answer is the main clause's subject, it wants a participial phrase instead.

participial_and_appositive.name: fronted participial phrase
participial_and_appositive.definition: A participial phrase placed before the main clause and modifying its subject.
participial_and_appositive.example: Turning the envelope over twice, she still did not open it.
participial_and_appositive.effect: Delays the subject and creates a moment of held attention before the clause resolves.
participial_and_appositive.caution: Its subject must be the main clause's subject, or it dangles.

participial_and_appositive.name: medial participial phrase
participial_and_appositive.definition: A participial phrase set between subject and verb, interrupting the clause it modifies.
participial_and_appositive.example: The pilot, checking the gauge a second time, said nothing to the passengers.
participial_and_appositive.effect: Slows the sentence exactly where the subject is under scrutiny.

participial_and_appositive.name: trailing participial phrase
participial_and_appositive.definition: A participial phrase attached after the main clause, extending it rightward.
participial_and_appositive.example: He walked the length of the platform, counting the doors as he went.
participial_and_appositive.effect: Keeps the sentence moving past its grammatical end; the engine of right-branching, cumulative prose.

participial_and_appositive.name: perfect participial phrase
participial_and_appositive.definition: A participial phrase headed by 'having' plus a past participle, marking its action as completed before the main clause.
participial_and_appositive.example: Having read the file twice, she asked for the pages that were missing.
participial_and_appositive.effect: Establishes prior action without a 'after' clause and without the past perfect's heaviness.
participial_and_appositive.caution: Two in a row builds an audit-report rhythm.

participial_and_appositive.name: passive participial phrase
participial_and_appositive.definition: A phrase headed by a past participle with passive sense, modifying a noun that undergoes the action.
participial_and_appositive.example: Stripped of its bark, the trunk showed the beetle tracks underneath.
participial_and_appositive.effect: Puts the affected thing forward and leaves the agent unnamed.

participial_and_appositive.name: reduced relative clause
participial_and_appositive.definition: A relative clause with its relative pronoun and copula removed, leaving a bare participial or prepositional modifier after the noun.
participial_and_appositive.example: The man standing by the door had been there since noon.
participial_and_appositive.effect: Trims four words without losing the modification; the cheapest available compression in English.
participial_and_appositive.caution: Reduced relatives create garden paths ('the horse raced past the barn fell'); read the sentence cold before keeping one.

participial_and_appositive.name: dangling participle
participial_and_appositive.definition: A participial phrase whose implied subject differs from the subject of the clause it attaches to.
participial_and_appositive.example: Faulty: 'Walking into the hearing, the microphone was already live.' Repaired: 'Walking into the hearing, she found the microphone already live.'
participial_and_appositive.effect: Produces an unintended and often comic attachment; the standard reason editors distrust fronted participles.
participial_and_appositive.caution: The fix is almost never to delete the phrase — it is to give the main clause the right subject.

participial_and_appositive.name: squinting modifier
participial_and_appositive.definition: A modifier placed between two elements it could plausibly modify, so the sentence supports two readings.
participial_and_appositive.example: Ambiguous: 'Reading the memo quickly angered him.' Repaired: 'Reading the memo made him angry at once.'
participial_and_appositive.effect: Named as a failure mode of medial placement; the cure is to move the modifier to an unambiguous slot.

participial_and_appositive.name: close appositive
participial_and_appositive.definition: A restrictive noun phrase set immediately beside another with no commas, narrowing rather than describing.
participial_and_appositive.example: My brother Tom never learned to swim.
participial_and_appositive.effect: Identifies which one; the absence of commas carries the restriction.
participial_and_appositive.caution: Comma placement is meaning: 'my brother, Tom,' implies there is only one brother.

participial_and_appositive.name: loose appositive
participial_and_appositive.definition: A non-restrictive noun phrase set off by commas, dashes, or parentheses, renaming the noun and adding information.
participial_and_appositive.example: The auditor, a woman who had spent nine years on bank failures, asked for the ledgers first.
participial_and_appositive.effect: Delivers characterization or credential without a separate clause or a 'who was'.

participial_and_appositive.name: fronted appositive
participial_and_appositive.definition: An appositive placed before the noun it renames, so the description arrives before the identity.
participial_and_appositive.example: A courthouse reporter for thirty years, Hallett had never seen a jury sequestered twice.
participial_and_appositive.effect: Withholds the name a beat, giving the description independent weight.
participial_and_appositive.caution: A newsroom staple; overuse marks the profile-piece register.

participial_and_appositive.name: appositive series
participial_and_appositive.definition: Three or more appositives in sequence renaming one noun.
participial_and_appositive.example: He had one asset left: the house, a leaking roof, a mortgage, an argument waiting to happen.
participial_and_appositive.effect: Accumulates perspectives on a single thing, each recasting the last.

participial_and_appositive.name: sentence appositive
participial_and_appositive.definition: A noun phrase in apposition not to a single noun but to the whole preceding clause, naming what the clause amounts to.
participial_and_appositive.example: The plant ran three shifts through the whole recession, a fact the town repeated to itself for years.
participial_and_appositive.effect: Lets the writer name the significance of an event without shifting into a 'which was' clause.

participial_and_appositive.name: resumptive modifier
participial_and_appositive.definition: A modifier that repeats a key word just used, then extends it with new material.
participial_and_appositive.example: They were left with a choice, a choice that neither side could afford to name out loud.
participial_and_appositive.effect: Marks the word as load-bearing and buys a second run at it; the natural cure for a clause that ended too soon.
participial_and_appositive.register: neutral to literary; effective in argument as well as narrative
participial_and_appositive.caution: Reads as padding if the extension adds nothing the first mention lacked.

participial_and_appositive.name: summative modifier
participial_and_appositive.definition: A modifier that sums up the preceding clause in a fresh noun and then elaborates on that noun.
participial_and_appositive.example: Deposits fell for six straight quarters, a decline the board attributed to weather.
participial_and_appositive.effect: Names the pattern the clause described, converting event into concept, then comments on it.
participial_and_appositive.register: especially useful in expository and argumentative prose

participial_and_appositive.name: free modifier
participial_and_appositive.definition: Any modifier (participial, absolute, appositive, adjectival) attached loosely to a base clause and movable within it — the building unit of Christensen's cumulative sentence.
participial_and_appositive.example: She read the file straight through, page after page, marking nothing, her coffee going cold beside her.
participial_and_appositive.effect: Adds levels of specificity below the base clause; the sentence deepens rather than lengthening sideways.

participial_and_appositive.name: trailing adjective phrase
participial_and_appositive.definition: An adjective or adjective pair moved out of prenominal position to the end of the clause.
participial_and_appositive.example: He came in from the yard, wet and unapologetic.
participial_and_appositive.effect: Gives the adjectives stress they would never get before the noun.

participial_and_appositive.name: fronted adjective phrase
participial_and_appositive.definition: An adjective phrase placed before the subject it modifies.
participial_and_appositive.example: Tired and three hours late, the delegation asked for coffee before anything else.
participial_and_appositive.effect: Establishes state before action, and varies openers away from the subject slot.

participial_and_appositive.name: postpositive adjective
participial_and_appositive.definition: An adjective placed after the noun it modifies, a survival of French and legal word order.
participial_and_appositive.example: It was the only course available, and everyone in the room knew it.
participial_and_appositive.effect: Formal, slightly ceremonial; also the only option with some indefinite pronouns ('something useful').

participial_and_appositive.name: epexegetical apposition
participial_and_appositive.definition: Apposition introduced by an explanatory marker — 'that is', 'namely', 'in other words' — restating the head in clearer or narrower terms.
participial_and_appositive.example: The bank failed for the usual reason, namely that it had lent short-term money on long-term promises.
participial_and_appositive.effect: Buys a plain-language gloss without a new sentence; the workhorse of technical exposition.
participial_and_appositive.caution: Three in a page make the prose feel like it is correcting itself.

participial_and_appositive.name: delayed appositive with dash
participial_and_appositive.definition: An appositive held to the end of the sentence and introduced by a dash, so the renaming lands as a punchline.
participial_and_appositive.example: Only one line in the budget had grown every year for a decade — interest.
participial_and_appositive.effect: Converts apposition into revelation by exploiting end-focus.
participial_and_appositive.caution: Loses force fast when repeated; one per section.

participial_and_appositive.name: gerund phrase as subject
participial_and_appositive.definition: An -ing clause occupying the subject slot of a sentence.
participial_and_appositive.example: Getting the ledgers out of the building took two days and a court order.
participial_and_appositive.effect: Nominalizes an action so it can be talked about as a thing.
participial_and_appositive.caution: Heavy gerund subjects push the verb far right; consider extraposition instead.

participial_and_appositive.name: purpose infinitive phrase
participial_and_appositive.definition: An infinitive clause functioning as an adjunct of purpose, fronted or trailing.
participial_and_appositive.example: To keep the account open, she moved money in on the last day of every month.
participial_and_appositive.effect: States the motive before the act, which is how motive is usually discovered in narrative.

participial_and_appositive.name: noun phrase in apposition to a pronoun
participial_and_appositive.definition: An appositive attached to a pronoun rather than a full noun phrase, usually to unpack it.
participial_and_appositive.example: They, the three who had signed the letter, were not invited back.
participial_and_appositive.effect: Adds specification to a pronoun that would otherwise be unrecoverable.
participial_and_appositive.register: formal; in fiction it reads as deliberate emphasis

sentence_architectures.name: simple sentence
sentence_architectures.definition: A sentence containing one independent clause and no subordinate clause, however long its phrases.
sentence_architectures.example: The river took the bridge in under an hour.
sentence_architectures.effect: Delivers one proposition with no hierarchy; used in series it reads as flat, declarative certainty.

sentence_architectures.name: compound sentence
sentence_architectures.definition: Two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction, semicolon, or colon.
sentence_architectures.example: The alarm sounded at four, and nobody in the building moved.
sentence_architectures.effect: Puts two facts on the same grammatical level, which implies they carry equal weight.

sentence_architectures.name: complex sentence
sentence_architectures.definition: One independent clause plus at least one subordinate clause.
sentence_architectures.example: Although the alarm sounded at four, nobody in the building moved.
sentence_architectures.effect: Ranks the propositions: the subordinate clause becomes background and the main clause becomes the point.

sentence_architectures.name: compound-complex sentence
sentence_architectures.definition: Two or more independent clauses with at least one subordinate clause attached.
sentence_architectures.example: The alarm sounded at four, and because nobody had run the drill in a year, the floor emptied in the wrong direction.
sentence_architectures.effect: Carries argument and background in one span; the standard load-bearing sentence of expository prose.
sentence_architectures.caution: Beyond about forty words it needs a short sentence after it.

sentence_architectures.name: periodic sentence
sentence_architectures.definition: A sentence that withholds its main clause — or the completion of it — until the end, so the sense is suspended until the final words.
sentence_architectures.example: Because the ledgers were incomplete, because two auditors had already resigned, and because the deadline was a week out, the board did the one thing nobody had proposed: nothing.
sentence_architectures.effect: Builds pressure and lands emphasis at the close; the reader must hold everything until the release.
sentence_architectures.caution: Two in succession exhaust the reader's short-term memory; alternate with loose sentences.

sentence_architectures.name: loose sentence
sentence_architectures.definition: A sentence that completes its main clause early and then adds modifying material, so it could grammatically stop at several points.
sentence_architectures.example: She left the hearing early, without a statement, without her lawyer, without looking at the row where the family sat.
sentence_architectures.effect: Feels natural and speech-like; meaning arrives immediately and detail accumulates after.
sentence_architectures.register: neutral; the default shape of modern English prose

sentence_architectures.name: cumulative sentence
sentence_architectures.definition: Christensen's refinement of the loose sentence: a short base clause followed by free modifiers at descending levels of generality, each adding texture to what precedes it.
sentence_architectures.example: The engine caught, coughing twice, settling into a rhythm that shook the whole frame, the mirror trembling with it.
sentence_architectures.effect: Renders perception in the order it happens: the fact first, then the noticing.
sentence_architectures.caution: The modifiers must descend in generality; a flat list is just a list.

sentence_architectures.name: balanced sentence
sentence_architectures.definition: A sentence whose parts are of equal grammatical structure and roughly equal length, set against or beside each other.
sentence_architectures.example: The first audit found nothing; the second found everything the first had walked past.
sentence_architectures.effect: Produces the sense of a considered judgment; symmetry reads as authority.
sentence_architectures.caution: Balanced sentences sound wise even when they are not; test whether the symmetry is doing argument or decoration.

sentence_architectures.name: left-branching sentence
sentence_architectures.definition: A sentence that piles modifying material before the subject and verb.
sentence_architectures.example: After two winters of hearings, after the third set of consultants, after the money ran out, the council voted.
sentence_architectures.effect: Front-loads context and delays action; formal, weighty, and effortful to read in quantity.
sentence_architectures.caution: English is natively right-branching; sustained left-branching reads as translationese.

sentence_architectures.name: right-branching sentence
sentence_architectures.definition: A sentence that states subject and verb first and appends modifying material afterward.
sentence_architectures.example: The council voted, after two winters of hearings, with three members absent and no money left in the fund.
sentence_architectures.effect: Easiest shape for a reader to process; the sentence is comprehensible from the first few words.

sentence_architectures.name: mid-branching sentence
sentence_architectures.definition: A sentence with modifying material embedded between subject and verb, so the predicate is held off in the middle.
sentence_architectures.example: The council, having spent two winters on hearings and most of the fund on consultants, voted.
sentence_architectures.effect: Creates suspension inside the clause; used sparingly it produces a formal, judicial poise.
sentence_architectures.caution: Deep center-embedding ('the rat the cat the dog chased killed ate') is the one shape human parsers genuinely fail on.

sentence_architectures.name: freight-train sentence
sentence_architectures.definition: A long chain of independent clauses coupled by coordinating conjunctions, with no subordination and no hierarchy.
sentence_architectures.example: The rain started and the field flooded and the trucks bogged down and the whole harvest sat there turning black.
sentence_architectures.effect: Everything on one level, one thing after another; produces momentum and a sense of events outrunning judgment.
sentence_architectures.caution: A signature move — powerful once per chapter, exhausting per page.

sentence_architectures.name: suspensive sentence
sentence_architectures.definition: A sentence whose completion is deferred by an interruption after the subject or after an auxiliary, so the reader waits for the resolving element.
sentence_architectures.example: The commissioner — a man who had survived four administrations, two indictments, and one televised apology — declined to comment.
sentence_architectures.effect: Holds the sentence open; whatever finally lands takes the accumulated pressure.

sentence_architectures.name: segregating style
sentence_architectures.definition: A sentence style built from short, mostly simple sentences with minimal coordination or subordination.
sentence_architectures.example: The plant closed in March. Nobody had warned the town. The parking lot stayed full for a week anyway.
sentence_architectures.effect: Reads as flat, controlled, and slightly withholding; the reader supplies the connective logic the syntax refuses.
sentence_architectures.caution: Sustained too long it flattens emphasis: everything shouts, so nothing does.

sentence_architectures.name: serial-predicate sentence
sentence_architectures.definition: One subject governing a chain of verbs with no repeated subject and often no conjunction until the last.
sentence_architectures.example: The wind rose, shifted, dropped, and came back stronger from the other side of the valley.
sentence_architectures.effect: Compresses a sequence into one continuous motion; the subject stays fixed while events run through it.

sentence_architectures.name: base clause with free modifiers
sentence_architectures.definition: The structural frame of cumulative prose: a grammatically complete main clause plus attachable modifiers that can be added, moved, or cut without breaking it.
sentence_architectures.effect: Gives the writer a revision handle — the base clause carries the meaning, the modifiers carry the texture, and they can be tuned independently.
sentence_architectures.example: He waited (base clause), hat in hand (absolute), saying nothing (participial), a man who had already been told no twice (appositive).

sentence_architectures.name: end-weight
sentence_architectures.definition: The principle that long and structurally heavy constituents belong at the end of the clause, short ones at the front.
sentence_architectures.example: Heavy: 'That the fund had been empty since March was obvious.' End-weighted: 'It was obvious that the fund had been empty since March.'
sentence_architectures.effect: Keeps the reader from holding a long subject in memory before the verb arrives; the main reason extraposition and passives exist.

sentence_architectures.name: end-focus
sentence_architectures.definition: The principle that new or emphatic information belongs at the end of the clause, where English puts its intonational peak.
sentence_architectures.example: Given a paragraph about the auditor: 'The ledgers were finally handed over by the auditor' is wrong-focused; 'The auditor finally handed over the ledgers' is right.
sentence_architectures.effect: Governs which of two grammatical orders is the right one; most 'flat' sentences are end-focus failures rather than word-choice failures.

sentence_architectures.name: front-loaded sentence
sentence_architectures.definition: A sentence with a long, complex subject before a short predicate.
sentence_architectures.example: Everyone who had signed the original petition, plus two who claimed they had, showed up.
sentence_architectures.effect: Builds anticipation for a small verb, which can land as a joke or as anticlimax.
sentence_architectures.caution: Usually a symptom of an unextraposed clause; check whether 'it' should take the subject slot.

sentence_architectures.name: topic-comment sentence
sentence_architectures.definition: A sentence that names its topic first as a separate constituent, then predicates something about it.
sentence_architectures.example: As for the missing deposits, no one has offered even an implausible explanation.
sentence_architectures.effect: Signals a shift of subject matter explicitly, which helps readers navigate long expositions.

sentence_architectures.name: loose-periodic hybrid
sentence_architectures.definition: A sentence that suspends its main clause once, resolves it, and then continues with trailing modifiers.
sentence_architectures.example: After nine days of testimony, the jury asked one question, a question about the dates, which nobody in the room had expected.
sentence_architectures.effect: Combines the pressure of the periodic opening with the ease of a loose close; the most common shape in accomplished long-sentence prose.

coordination_and_subordination.name: parataxis
coordination_and_subordination.definition: The placing of clauses side by side with no explicit marker of their logical relation.
coordination_and_subordination.example: The letter came on Tuesday. She read it once. She did not go to work that week.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Refuses to rank or explain; the reader infers cause, and inference feels like discovery.
coordination_and_subordination.caution: In argument, parataxis can look like an argument that has not been made.

coordination_and_subordination.name: hypotaxis
coordination_and_subordination.definition: The subordination of clauses to one another with explicit markers, producing a hierarchy of main and dependent material.
coordination_and_subordination.example: She did not go to work that week because the letter had said, in a sentence she reread until she knew it, that the appeal was over.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: States the logical relations rather than implying them; the natural mode of analysis and argument.
coordination_and_subordination.caution: Stacked hypotaxis buries the main clause; keep the load-bearing claim in the main slot.

coordination_and_subordination.name: asyndetic coordination
coordination_and_subordination.definition: Coordination with the conjunctions omitted between the coordinated elements.
coordination_and_subordination.example: They took the files, the drives, the phones off every desk on the floor.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Speeds the series and implies it could continue; the list feels partial rather than closed.

coordination_and_subordination.name: polysyndetic coordination
coordination_and_subordination.definition: Coordination with a conjunction between every element, including where one would normally be omitted.
coordination_and_subordination.example: They took the files and the drives and the phones and the sticky notes off the monitors.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Slows the series and weights each item equally; produces either childlike accumulation or biblical gravity.

coordination_and_subordination.name: syndetic coordination
coordination_and_subordination.definition: Ordinary coordination with a single conjunction before the final element of a series.
coordination_and_subordination.example: The report named the bank, the auditor, and the two directors who had signed.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: The unmarked baseline; its neutrality is what makes asyndeton and polysyndeton audible.

coordination_and_subordination.name: correlative coordination
coordination_and_subordination.definition: Coordination using a paired marker — both…and, either…or, neither…nor, not only…but also — that announces the second element in advance.
coordination_and_subordination.example: The fund lost not only the quarter's gains but also the reserve it had been holding since the merger.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Sets up an expectation and then satisfies it; useful for escalation.
coordination_and_subordination.caution: The elements after each marker must be grammatically parallel, or the sentence audibly limps.

coordination_and_subordination.name: comparative correlative
coordination_and_subordination.definition: The paired-comparative construction 'the more X, the more Y', expressing covariation in two dependent clauses.
coordination_and_subordination.example: The longer the hearing ran, the fewer questions anyone asked.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Compresses a whole causal relationship into one shape; aphoristic by default.
coordination_and_subordination.caution: Its aphoristic ring makes weak generalizations sound proven.

coordination_and_subordination.name: fronted adverbial clause
coordination_and_subordination.definition: A subordinate adverbial clause placed before the main clause.
coordination_and_subordination.example: Because the vote had already been counted, the objection changed nothing.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Frames the main clause with its condition; the reader reads the main clause already knowing how to take it.

coordination_and_subordination.name: trailing adverbial clause
coordination_and_subordination.definition: A subordinate adverbial clause placed after the main clause.
coordination_and_subordination.example: The objection changed nothing, because the vote had already been counted.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Gives the main clause the front position and the subordinate one the end-focus slot; often the better default in argument.

coordination_and_subordination.name: concessive clause
coordination_and_subordination.definition: A subordinate clause conceding something that might be expected to block the main clause: although, though, even though, while, granted that.
coordination_and_subordination.example: Although the numbers were public the whole time, no one had put two of them side by side.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Anticipates and absorbs an objection inside the sentence; the syntactic form of intellectual honesty.

coordination_and_subordination.name: conditional clause
coordination_and_subordination.definition: A subordinate clause stating a condition on which the main clause depends: if, unless, provided that, as long as.
coordination_and_subordination.example: If the reserve was already spent in March, the March statement was false.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Puts the reader inside a hypothetical, which is how arguments test claims without asserting them.

coordination_and_subordination.name: inverted conditional
coordination_and_subordination.definition: A conditional with 'if' deleted and the auxiliary raised before the subject.
coordination_and_subordination.example: Had she asked for the ledgers a month earlier, the auditor would still have had them.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Compresses and formalizes; the raised auxiliary carries a literary or legal weight that 'if' does not.
coordination_and_subordination.caution: In casual registers it reads as costume.

coordination_and_subordination.name: causal clause
coordination_and_subordination.definition: A subordinate clause giving the reason for the main clause: because, since, as, in that, seeing that.
coordination_and_subordination.example: The town kept the plant on its letterhead for a decade, since nothing else had ever been printed there.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: States causation explicitly, which is either honest or presumptuous depending on the evidence behind it.
coordination_and_subordination.caution: 'Since' and 'as' are ambiguous between causal and temporal readings; prefer 'because' when the logic matters.

coordination_and_subordination.name: temporal clause
coordination_and_subordination.definition: A subordinate clause locating the main clause in time: when, while, before, after, until, as soon as, once.
coordination_and_subordination.example: By the time the auditors arrived, the server room had been emptied and repainted.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Sequences events without a separate sentence, and lets the writer skip over intervening time.

coordination_and_subordination.name: purpose clause
coordination_and_subordination.definition: A subordinate clause stating the intended result of the main clause: so that, in order that, lest.
coordination_and_subordination.example: They filed the amendment on a Friday so that the story would break over a weekend.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Attributes intention, which raises the evidentiary bar the sentence must clear.

coordination_and_subordination.name: result clause
coordination_and_subordination.definition: A subordinate clause stating an actual consequence, typically correlated with 'so' or 'such' in the main clause.
coordination_and_subordination.example: The room was so cold that the stenographer typed in gloves.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Makes a degree concrete by naming what it caused — the standard cure for an unearned intensifier.

coordination_and_subordination.name: comparative clause
coordination_and_subordination.definition: A subordinate clause completing a comparison: than, as…as, the same…as.
coordination_and_subordination.example: The second audit cost more than the shortfall it was hired to explain.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Puts two magnitudes in one frame; a comparison is often the shortest available argument.
coordination_and_subordination.caution: Comparative clauses invite deletion errors — check that both terms are actually stated.

coordination_and_subordination.name: restrictive relative clause
coordination_and_subordination.definition: A relative clause that narrows the reference of its head noun, written without commas.
coordination_and_subordination.example: The directors who had signed the March statement resigned within a week.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Identifies which members of a set are meant; deleting it changes the sentence's claim.
coordination_and_subordination.caution: Commas around it silently convert the claim from 'some' to 'all'.

coordination_and_subordination.name: non-restrictive relative clause
coordination_and_subordination.definition: A relative clause that adds information about an already-identified head, set off by commas.
coordination_and_subordination.example: The March statement, which the directors had all signed, was withdrawn in April.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Slips a second predication into the sentence at low cost.
coordination_and_subordination.caution: It is parenthetical: the sentence must still work if it is cut.

coordination_and_subordination.name: sentential relative clause
coordination_and_subordination.definition: A 'which' clause whose antecedent is the entire preceding clause rather than any noun in it.
coordination_and_subordination.pattern: [Main clause], which [comment on the whole clause]
coordination_and_subordination.example: The board met twice in one week, which had not happened since the merger.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Comments on an event as a whole; the conversational cousin of the summative modifier.
coordination_and_subordination.caution: Ambiguity risk — if a noun could be the antecedent, use a summative noun instead.

coordination_and_subordination.name: free relative clause
coordination_and_subordination.definition: A relative clause with no separate head noun, the wh-word carrying both the head and the relative function.
coordination_and_subordination.example: What the ledgers showed was a bank that had been insolvent for two years.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Packages an entire proposition as a noun phrase; the raw material of the pseudo-cleft.

coordination_and_subordination.name: that-clause complement
coordination_and_subordination.definition: A finite subordinate clause functioning as the subject, object, or complement of the main verb.
coordination_and_subordination.example: The examiner concluded that the reserve had never existed in the form reported.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Marks the proposition as reported or attributed rather than asserted directly — the basic syntax of citation.

coordination_and_subordination.name: stacked subordination
coordination_and_subordination.definition: Successive subordinate clauses each embedded in the previous one.
coordination_and_subordination.example: They cited a rule that referred to a schedule that had been repealed by a statute nobody had reprinted.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Enacts bureaucratic depth; used deliberately it is comedy, used accidentally it is opacity.
coordination_and_subordination.caution: Three levels is the practical ceiling in prose meant to be read once.

coordination_and_subordination.name: upside-down subordination
coordination_and_subordination.definition: Placing the sentence's most important content in a subordinate clause and something trivial in the main clause.
coordination_and_subordination.example: Weak: 'It was in 2011 that the fund, which lost every dollar of the reserve, was audited.' Repaired: 'The 2011 audit found that the fund had lost every dollar of the reserve.'
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Named as a diagnostic: the syntax is telling the reader the wrong thing matters.
coordination_and_subordination.caution: Test each long sentence by reading only its main clause; if that sentence is not the point, restructure.

coordination_and_subordination.name: comma splice
coordination_and_subordination.definition: Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone, used deliberately for pace or closeness.
coordination_and_subordination.example: She did not argue, she signed.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Binds two clauses more tightly than a period and more casually than a semicolon.
coordination_and_subordination.caution: One deliberate splice per chapter reads as style; two per page reads as an error the copy editor missed.

coordination_and_subordination.name: semicolon coordination
coordination_and_subordination.definition: Joining independent clauses with a semicolon, leaving the logical relation unstated but the connection asserted.
coordination_and_subordination.example: The first audit found nothing; the second was not conducted by the same firm.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Implies relevance without naming the relation — the reader supplies 'and yet' or 'because'.

coordination_and_subordination.name: colon as logical connector
coordination_and_subordination.definition: A colon joining a clause to what follows as its explanation, expansion, or instance.
coordination_and_subordination.example: The answer was in the footnote: the reserve had been reclassified in March.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Promises a payoff and delivers it in the same sentence; the most efficient reveal punctuation has.
coordination_and_subordination.caution: The material before the colon should be a complete clause in formal prose.

coordination_and_subordination.name: conjunctive adverb linkage
coordination_and_subordination.definition: Linking independent clauses or sentences with an adverbial connector — however, therefore, moreover, nevertheless — rather than a conjunction.
coordination_and_subordination.example: The bank met every ratio it reported; the ratios, however, were computed on the wrong denominator.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Names the logical relation while keeping the clauses grammatically independent.
coordination_and_subordination.caution: Sentence-initial 'however' plus comma is the most overused connective in expository prose; move it inside the clause or use 'but'.

coordination_and_subordination.name: sentence-initial conjunction
coordination_and_subordination.definition: Beginning a sentence with 'and', 'but', 'or', or 'so', coordinating across the period.
coordination_and_subordination.example: The board had the memo in October. But nobody moved on it until the following spring.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Splits a compound sentence into two beats while keeping the coordination audible; adds speech rhythm.
coordination_and_subordination.register: neutral to informal; standard in contemporary nonfiction
coordination_and_subordination.caution: The prohibition against it is a schoolroom myth, but the effect dulls with repetition.

coordination_and_subordination.name: conjunction reduction
coordination_and_subordination.definition: Coordination in which a shared element — usually the subject or auxiliary — is stated once and understood in the following conjuncts.
coordination_and_subordination.example: The examiner opened the file, read for ten minutes, and asked for the previous year's.
coordination_and_subordination.effect: Keeps the subject in focus while the verbs accumulate; the ordinary alternative to repeating a noun.

focus_constructions.name: it-cleft
focus_constructions.definition: A construction splitting one clause into two, with dummy 'it' plus a copula highlighting one element and the remainder relegated to a relative-like clause.
focus_constructions.pattern: It was [focused element] that/who [rest of clause]
focus_constructions.example: It was the March statement, not the audit, that finally forced the resignations.
focus_constructions.effect: Puts contrastive stress on the focused element in writing, where intonation is unavailable.
focus_constructions.register: neutral; heavily used in argument and courtroom prose
focus_constructions.caution: Clefting an element nobody was contesting makes the prose sound argumentative for no reason.

focus_constructions.name: wh-cleft
focus_constructions.definition: A cleft whose first half is a free relative and whose second half is the focused element, joined by 'is' or 'was'.
focus_constructions.example: What the ledgers showed was a reserve that had been counted twice.
focus_constructions.effect: Delays the news to the end of the sentence, where it takes the natural stress; useful for controlled reveals.
focus_constructions.caution: Common padding in speech-derived prose ('what I would say is that…'); keep it when the delay earns something.

focus_constructions.name: reversed wh-cleft
focus_constructions.definition: A pseudo-cleft with the order inverted, the focused element first and the free relative last.
focus_constructions.example: A reserve counted twice is what the ledgers showed.
focus_constructions.effect: Puts the news first and the frame after; more emphatic and more conversational than the standard order.

focus_constructions.name: all-cleft
focus_constructions.definition: A cleft whose free relative is headed by 'all', restricting the claim to exactly one thing.
focus_constructions.example: All the committee ever asked for was a list of the accounts.
focus_constructions.effect: Adds the sense of 'and nothing more' — minimization, complaint, or modesty depending on context.

focus_constructions.name: th-cleft
focus_constructions.definition: A cleft whose first half is a definite noun phrase — 'the thing that', 'the reason why', 'the one who' — rather than a bare wh-word.
focus_constructions.example: The thing that finally moved the regulator was a single page of dates.
focus_constructions.effect: Names the category of the focused item as it announces it, which lets the writer characterize before revealing.

focus_constructions.name: inferential cleft
focus_constructions.definition: A cleft of the form 'it is (not) that…', used to correct or refine an inference the reader might draw.
focus_constructions.example: It is not that the directors ignored the memo; it is that nobody could say who had received it.
focus_constructions.effect: Rejects a likely misreading and substitutes a precise one — a compact concede-and-refine move.

focus_constructions.name: if-because cleft
focus_constructions.definition: A two-part construction pairing a conditional frame with a causal focus: 'If X, it's because Y.'
focus_constructions.example: If the town still argues about the closure, it is because nobody was ever told the reason for it.
focus_constructions.effect: Asserts an explanation while presupposing the situation, which makes the explanation harder to challenge.
focus_constructions.caution: The presupposition is doing rhetorical work; be sure it is one the reader has granted.

focus_constructions.name: existential there
focus_constructions.definition: A construction using non-referential 'there' as grammatical subject so the logical subject can follow the verb.
focus_constructions.example: There were two versions of the March statement in the file.
focus_constructions.effect: Introduces new entities into the discourse in the end-focus slot, where new information belongs.
focus_constructions.caution: The standard vice of flat prose is existential 'there' used where a real subject and verb were available.

focus_constructions.name: presentational construction
focus_constructions.definition: A construction that brings a new participant onstage, typically with 'there' plus a verb of appearance or motion rather than 'be'.
focus_constructions.example: There came, near the end of the second day, a question nobody on the panel had prepared for.
focus_constructions.effect: Stages an entrance; the delay before the noun functions as a drumroll.

focus_constructions.name: extraposition
focus_constructions.definition: Moving a heavy clausal subject to the end of the sentence and filling the subject slot with anticipatory 'it'.
focus_constructions.example: It was obvious by then that the reserve had never been segregated.
focus_constructions.effect: Satisfies end-weight, keeping the reader from parsing a long subject before the verb.
focus_constructions.caution: Extraposition plus a passive predicate ('it was decided that') erases the agent; check whether that is intended.

focus_constructions.name: fronting
focus_constructions.definition: Moving a non-subject constituent — object, complement, adverbial — to the front of the clause without inversion.
focus_constructions.example: The ledgers she handed over. The correspondence she did not.
focus_constructions.effect: Links the sentence to the preceding topic and puts the remainder in focus; the cheapest cohesion device in English.
focus_constructions.caution: Fronting a constituent the reader has no prior interest in produces mannerism, not emphasis.

focus_constructions.name: left dislocation
focus_constructions.definition: Announcing a topic as a detached noun phrase and then resuming it inside the clause with a pronoun.
focus_constructions.example: The two directors who signed, they were gone before the report was printed.
focus_constructions.effect: Speech-like topic-setting; gives the reader the subject before the sentence has to carry it.

focus_constructions.name: right dislocation
focus_constructions.definition: Using a pronoun in the clause and appending its referent as a detached noun phrase at the end.
focus_constructions.example: He never once returned a call, the man who had signed every one of those statements.
focus_constructions.effect: Afterthought clarification with an edge of contempt or affection depending on the noun phrase.

focus_constructions.name: negative inversion
focus_constructions.definition: Subject–auxiliary inversion triggered by a fronted negative or restrictive adverbial: never, rarely, not once, only then, under no circumstances.
focus_constructions.example: Not once in nine days did anyone ask where the money had gone.
focus_constructions.effect: Formal, emphatic, and slightly theatrical; the fronted negative takes maximum stress.
focus_constructions.caution: Two on a page and the prose starts declaiming.

focus_constructions.name: locative inversion
focus_constructions.definition: Fronting a locative or directional phrase and inverting subject and verb, so the subject arrives last.
focus_constructions.example: Behind the last row of filing cabinets sat the boxes the examiner had been asking for.
focus_constructions.effect: Moves the camera and then reveals what is there; end-focus applied to physical discovery.
focus_constructions.caution: Works only with intransitive verbs of position or motion; forcing it elsewhere sounds wrong.

focus_constructions.name: directional inversion
focus_constructions.definition: Inversion after a short directional adverb, with the verb before the subject.
focus_constructions.example: Down came the ceiling tiles, one corner of the room at a time.
focus_constructions.effect: Kinetic, slightly archaic; foregrounds the motion over the mover.

focus_constructions.name: so-inversion
focus_constructions.definition: Inversion after a fronted 'so' or 'such' plus a degree expression, with the result clause following.
focus_constructions.example: So thin was the file that the clerk asked twice whether it was the whole record.
focus_constructions.effect: Elevated intensification; the degree lands before the thing it describes.
focus_constructions.caution: Firmly marked as 'writerly' — one per chapter at most.

focus_constructions.name: agentless passive
focus_constructions.definition: A passive clause with no by-phrase, so the affected entity takes the subject slot and the agent goes unnamed.
focus_constructions.example: The March statement was withdrawn without explanation.
focus_constructions.effect: Focuses on the event and its object; legitimately used when the agent is unknown, irrelevant, or obvious.
focus_constructions.caution: Also the standard syntax of evasion — check whether the missing agent is missing because you do not know it or because naming it would be inconvenient.

focus_constructions.name: passive with by-phrase
focus_constructions.definition: A full passive that keeps the agent but moves it to the end of the clause.
focus_constructions.example: The reserve had been reclassified by the same officer who signed the audit letter.
focus_constructions.effect: Reorders for cohesion and end-focus: known thing first, newsworthy agent last.
focus_constructions.register: neutral; the legitimate answer to blanket anti-passive advice

focus_constructions.name: heavy NP shift
focus_constructions.definition: Moving a long object noun phrase past a shorter constituent to the end of the clause.
focus_constructions.example: She handed to the clerk every page the examiner had asked for and several he had not.
focus_constructions.effect: Restores end-weight when the object is longer than what follows it.
focus_constructions.caution: With a short object it sounds broken; the shift needs the weight to justify it.

focus_constructions.name: particle shift
focus_constructions.definition: The alternation in phrasal verbs between 'verb particle object' and 'verb object particle'.
focus_constructions.example: 'She turned the offer down' foregrounds the offer; 'she turned down the offer' foregrounds the refusal.
focus_constructions.effect: A free choice that tunes emphasis and rhythm; with a pronoun object, only the first order is grammatical.

focus_constructions.name: dative alternation
focus_constructions.definition: The choice between a double-object construction and a prepositional dative.
focus_constructions.example: 'He gave the committee his notes' ends on the notes; 'he gave his notes to the committee' ends on the committee.
focus_constructions.effect: Decides which of two arguments takes end-focus; usually a cohesion decision, not a stylistic one.

focus_constructions.name: subject-to-subject raising
focus_constructions.definition: A construction where the subject of an embedded clause surfaces as the subject of the main verb ('seem', 'appear', 'happen', 'turn out').
focus_constructions.example: The reserve appears to have been spent in two transactions.
focus_constructions.effect: Hedges an assertion while keeping the entity in the subject slot; the workhorse hedge of careful nonfiction.
focus_constructions.caution: Stacked raising verbs ('seems to tend to appear to') is pure evasion.

focus_constructions.name: tough-movement
focus_constructions.definition: A construction in which the object of an embedded infinitive becomes the subject of an adjective like 'hard', 'easy', 'impossible'.
focus_constructions.example: That paragraph is easy to misread and hard to defend.
focus_constructions.effect: Puts the thing being judged in the subject slot rather than the judging.

focus_constructions.name: emphatic do
focus_constructions.definition: Insertion of the auxiliary 'do' in an affirmative declarative to contradict, insist, or concede.
focus_constructions.example: The board did meet in October; what it did not do was write anything down.
focus_constructions.effect: The written substitute for contrastive stress; concedes a point before qualifying it.
focus_constructions.caution: Only works against a contrary expectation; without one it reads as filler.

focus_constructions.name: cataphoric opening
focus_constructions.definition: Opening with a pronoun or pro-form whose referent is withheld until later in the sentence or passage.
focus_constructions.example: It arrived in a plain envelope, unsigned, and it ended three careers: the memo.
focus_constructions.effect: Creates a small suspense by making the reader wait to learn what is being discussed.
focus_constructions.caution: Sustained cataphora is annoying rather than intriguing; resolve it inside a sentence or two.

focus_constructions.name: object fronting for contrast
focus_constructions.definition: Fronting an object specifically to set it against a parallel element in an adjacent clause.
focus_constructions.example: The salaries the trustees would discuss; the fees they would not.
focus_constructions.effect: Makes contrast structural rather than lexical — no 'but' required.

ellipsis_and_compression.name: gapping
ellipsis_and_compression.definition: Omission of the repeated verb (and sometimes more) from the second of two coordinated clauses.
ellipsis_and_compression.example: Sarah ordered the fish; Marcus, the lamb.
ellipsis_and_compression.effect: Compresses parallel information and makes the contrast audible; the comma does the verb's work.
ellipsis_and_compression.caution: Requires strict parallelism; if the structures differ, the gap cannot be recovered.

ellipsis_and_compression.name: stripping
ellipsis_and_compression.definition: Reduction of the second conjunct to a single remnant, usually with 'too', 'either', or 'not'.
ellipsis_and_compression.example: The auditor resigned, and the deputy too.
ellipsis_and_compression.effect: Maximum compression of a repeated predicate; keeps the sentence moving.

ellipsis_and_compression.name: sluicing
ellipsis_and_compression.definition: Ellipsis of everything after a wh-word in an embedded or standalone question.
ellipsis_and_compression.example: Someone had already pulled the file, but nobody would say who.
ellipsis_and_compression.effect: Leaves the question open in the fewest possible words; the syntax of an unanswered question.

ellipsis_and_compression.name: VP-ellipsis
ellipsis_and_compression.definition: Omission of a verb phrase after an auxiliary that survives.
ellipsis_and_compression.example: She could have called the regulator that week. She didn't.
ellipsis_and_compression.effect: The most common English ellipsis; keeps a contrast sharp by removing everything the reader already has.

ellipsis_and_compression.name: pseudogapping
ellipsis_and_compression.definition: Ellipsis of the verb but not its object in the second clause, leaving a stranded remnant after the auxiliary.
ellipsis_and_compression.example: She will testify about the transfers, but she won't about the memo.
ellipsis_and_compression.effect: A colloquial halfway house between gapping and VP-ellipsis; sounds spoken.

ellipsis_and_compression.name: comparative deletion
ellipsis_and_compression.definition: Omission of the repeated material in the second term of a comparison.
ellipsis_and_compression.example: The hearing produced more paper than answers.
ellipsis_and_compression.caution: Deleting too much creates the classic ambiguous comparative ('she trusts the auditor more than the board').

ellipsis_and_compression.name: verbless clause
ellipsis_and_compression.definition: A subordinate clause with the verb (usually a form of 'be') omitted.
ellipsis_and_compression.example: Though unable to name a single source, the reporter would not retract.
ellipsis_and_compression.effect: Formal compression; keeps the subordinate material from competing with the main clause.

ellipsis_and_compression.name: nominal sentence
ellipsis_and_compression.definition: A standalone sentence with no verb at all, consisting of a noun phrase or phrases.
ellipsis_and_compression.example: Nine days of testimony. One question at the end of it.
ellipsis_and_compression.effect: Presents an image or fact as a fixed state, outside time; strongly marked.
ellipsis_and_compression.caution: A stylistic signature; more than one or two per chapter and the prose starts posing.

ellipsis_and_compression.name: syntactic zeugma
ellipsis_and_compression.definition: One verb (or preposition) governing two or more complements it fits differently, often one literal and one figurative.
ellipsis_and_compression.example: He left the building, the payroll, and any claim to a pension in the same afternoon.
ellipsis_and_compression.effect: Compression plus wit; the yoking itself supplies the comment.
ellipsis_and_compression.caution: Reads as a joke whether or not you intended one — check the tone of the surrounding passage.

ellipsis_and_compression.name: subject ellipsis
ellipsis_and_compression.definition: Omission of the subject pronoun at the start of a clause, as in diaries, notes, and clipped narration.
ellipsis_and_compression.example: Called the office twice. Left no message either time.
ellipsis_and_compression.effect: Produces a private, note-to-self texture and speeds narration.
ellipsis_and_compression.register: informal, epistolary, diary, hard-boiled first person

ellipsis_and_compression.name: determiner omission
ellipsis_and_compression.definition: Dropping articles and other determiners for telegraphic compression.
ellipsis_and_compression.example: Bank closed Friday. Depositors notified Monday.
ellipsis_and_compression.effect: Headline or cable texture; urgency at the cost of nuance.
ellipsis_and_compression.caution: Extended past a line or two it becomes a costume rather than a style.

ellipsis_and_compression.name: right-node raising
ellipsis_and_compression.definition: Coordination in which two clauses share a final constituent, stated once at the end.
ellipsis_and_compression.pattern: [Subject A] [verb A], and [subject B] [verb B], [shared object]
ellipsis_and_compression.example: She drafted, and he signed, the letter that ended the inquiry.
ellipsis_and_compression.effect: Holds the shared element to the last position where it takes double stress.
ellipsis_and_compression.caution: The interrupting commas are essential; without them the sentence collapses.

ellipsis_and_compression.name: fragment answer
ellipsis_and_compression.definition: A reply consisting only of the constituent that answers the question, the rest of the clause elided.
ellipsis_and_compression.example: Who authorized it? Nobody anyone could name.
ellipsis_and_compression.effect: Natural dialogue rhythm; full-sentence answers in fiction sound like depositions.

ellipsis_and_compression.name: null-complement anaphora
ellipsis_and_compression.definition: Omission of an entire understood complement after verbs like 'refuse', 'agree', 'try', 'find out'.
ellipsis_and_compression.example: The committee asked him to name the officer. He refused.
ellipsis_and_compression.effect: Keeps the focus on the act rather than restating its content.

ellipsis_and_compression.name: that-deletion
ellipsis_and_compression.definition: Omission of the complementizer 'that' before a finite complement clause.
ellipsis_and_compression.example: She knew the file was incomplete before she opened it.
ellipsis_and_compression.effect: Lightens the sentence and speeds it; the default in speech and in most modern nonfiction.
ellipsis_and_compression.caution: Keep 'that' when the following words could be misparsed as the verb's object ('she knew the file was' vs 'she knew the file').

ellipsis_and_compression.name: zero relative
ellipsis_and_compression.definition: A restrictive relative clause with the relative pronoun omitted, possible when the pronoun is the object.
ellipsis_and_compression.example: The page she wanted had been removed from the binder.
ellipsis_and_compression.effect: Removes two syllables of scaffolding and tightens the noun phrase.
ellipsis_and_compression.caution: Impossible when the relative would be the subject: 'the page was missing' cannot become 'the page missing' without changing the structure.

ellipsis_and_compression.name: conversational deletion
ellipsis_and_compression.definition: Omission of sentence-initial function words — subjects, auxiliaries, articles — as they routinely drop in speech.
ellipsis_and_compression.example: Seen the March file? Not since Tuesday.
ellipsis_and_compression.effect: Renders spoken register on the page without phonetic spelling.

interruption_and_parenthesis.name: parenthesis
interruption_and_parenthesis.definition: Insertion of a grammatically independent element into a sentence, marked by round brackets.
interruption_and_parenthesis.example: The reserve (a number that appeared in only one document) was carried forward for three years.
interruption_and_parenthesis.effect: Signals subordinate status typographically: the reader knows this can be skipped.
interruption_and_parenthesis.caution: Brackets whisper; anything you want the reader to hear should not be in them.

interruption_and_parenthesis.name: parenthetical dash pair
interruption_and_parenthesis.definition: Insertion set off by a pair of em dashes rather than commas or brackets.
interruption_and_parenthesis.example: The examiner — who had asked for the ledgers twice in writing — went to the regulator instead.
interruption_and_parenthesis.effect: Louder than brackets, more abrupt than commas; the insertion keeps full emphasis.
interruption_and_parenthesis.caution: More than one dash pair per paragraph and the prose develops a stammer.

interruption_and_parenthesis.name: comma parenthesis
interruption_and_parenthesis.definition: The quietest insertion: parenthetical material set off with commas.
interruption_and_parenthesis.example: The March statement, as everyone later agreed, should never have been signed.
interruption_and_parenthesis.effect: Integrates the aside into the sentence's flow instead of interrupting it.
interruption_and_parenthesis.caution: Fails when the insertion is long enough that the reader loses the main clause.

interruption_and_parenthesis.name: comment clause
interruption_and_parenthesis.definition: A short parenthetical clause expressing the speaker's stance toward the proposition: I think, you know, it seems, one imagines.
interruption_and_parenthesis.example: The reclassification was, I think, the only decision anyone made deliberately.
interruption_and_parenthesis.effect: Adds a human speaking presence and hedges the claim at once.
interruption_and_parenthesis.caution: In argument these read as hedging; count them before a revision pass.

interruption_and_parenthesis.name: disjunct insertion
interruption_and_parenthesis.definition: Insertion of a sentence adverbial commenting on the truth or manner of the whole statement: frankly, admittedly, oddly enough.
interruption_and_parenthesis.example: The board, admittedly, had never been given the underlying schedule.
interruption_and_parenthesis.effect: Marks the writer's attitude to the claim without a separate sentence.

interruption_and_parenthesis.name: authorial aside
interruption_and_parenthesis.definition: A parenthetical remark in which the writer steps briefly outside the narrative or argument to address the reader directly.
interruption_and_parenthesis.example: The fund had by then been audited four times (four — I counted them in the docket) with no adverse finding.
interruption_and_parenthesis.effect: Establishes a companionable narrator; makes the writing feel like thinking rather than reporting.
interruption_and_parenthesis.register: essay, narrative nonfiction, voiced first person
interruption_and_parenthesis.caution: Each aside costs momentum; spend them on something the reader could not have supplied.

interruption_and_parenthesis.name: split dialogue tag
interruption_and_parenthesis.definition: A speech tag inserted mid-utterance, breaking the quoted line in two.
interruption_and_parenthesis.example: "I signed it," she said, "the way I signed everything that year."
interruption_and_parenthesis.effect: Places a beat exactly where the speaker would pause; controls dialogue rhythm without stage directions.
interruption_and_parenthesis.caution: Split at a natural breath, not mid-phrase, or the line reads as artificially interrupted.

interruption_and_parenthesis.name: trailing dash afterthought
interruption_and_parenthesis.definition: A single dash near the end of the sentence introducing a late addition or qualification.
interruption_and_parenthesis.example: Nobody could find the original — or wanted to.
interruption_and_parenthesis.effect: Mimics the mind adding something it had held back; often the sentence's sharpest content.
interruption_and_parenthesis.caution: Because it always lands hard, a weak afterthought is very visibly weak.

interruption_and_parenthesis.name: self-correction
interruption_and_parenthesis.definition: Mid-sentence repair, replacing a word or phrase just used: 'or rather', 'or, more precisely'.
interruption_and_parenthesis.example: The board approved the transfer — or rather, no one at the table objected to it.
interruption_and_parenthesis.effect: Enacts precision as a live process; the correction persuades more than the corrected version alone would.
interruption_and_parenthesis.caution: Real repairs only; performed hesitation is transparent.

interruption_and_parenthesis.name: anacoluthon
interruption_and_parenthesis.definition: A sentence that abandons one grammatical construction partway and continues in another.
interruption_and_parenthesis.example: The people who signed those statements, the fact is not one of them has explained why.
interruption_and_parenthesis.effect: Renders a mind overtaken by its own material; in dialogue and voiced narration it reads as authentic disruption.
interruption_and_parenthesis.caution: Indistinguishable from an editing error unless the surrounding prose is visibly controlled.

interruption_and_parenthesis.name: aposiopesis
interruption_and_parenthesis.definition: Construction sense: a clause abandoned before its grammar completes, marked by a dash and left without its predicate. The figure names the gesture; this names the sentence pattern.
interruption_and_parenthesis.example: If they had told anyone in the town what the numbers actually meant—
interruption_and_parenthesis.effect: The unsaid completion carries more than a stated one; used for menace, grief, or refusal.
interruption_and_parenthesis.caution: One per scene; a page of broken-off sentences reads as coyness.

interruption_and_parenthesis.name: vocative insertion
interruption_and_parenthesis.definition: A direct address to a person inserted into a clause and set off by commas.
interruption_and_parenthesis.example: You will find, reader, that the dates do not line up.
interruption_and_parenthesis.effect: Turns statement into address; in nonfiction the vocative 'reader' is a strong period marker.

interruption_and_parenthesis.name: tag question
interruption_and_parenthesis.definition: A short interrogative appended to a declarative, seeking or performing agreement.
interruption_and_parenthesis.example: They had every reason to check that number, didn't they.
interruption_and_parenthesis.effect: Pulls the reader into complicity, or renders a speaker fishing for confirmation.
interruption_and_parenthesis.caution: In nonfiction it can read as bullying the reader into assent.

interruption_and_parenthesis.name: interpolated question
interruption_and_parenthesis.definition: A question inserted into the middle of an otherwise declarative passage, in the writer's or a character's voice.
interruption_and_parenthesis.example: The deposits fell every quarter — who reads a quarterly statement four times running? — and nobody flagged it.
interruption_and_parenthesis.effect: Breaks exposition with a beat of live thought and licenses the answer that follows.

interruption_and_parenthesis.name: nested parenthesis
interruption_and_parenthesis.definition: A parenthetical element contained within another parenthetical element.
interruption_and_parenthesis.example: The letter (which arrived, as everything that year arrived (late), in a state courier envelope) was never entered in the log.
interruption_and_parenthesis.effect: Enacts digression and, in comic or pedantic voices, is the joke.
interruption_and_parenthesis.caution: Two levels is already a stunt; three is unreadable.

modifier_placement.name: fronted adverbial
modifier_placement.definition: An adverbial phrase placed before the subject, setting time, place, or condition for the clause.
modifier_placement.example: By the third week of hearings, the gallery had thinned to reporters and relatives.
modifier_placement.effect: Orients the reader before the action; the main way prose changes scene inside a paragraph.
modifier_placement.caution: A string of paragraphs opening this way flattens into a chronicle.

modifier_placement.name: medial adverbial
modifier_placement.definition: An adverbial placed between subject and verb or inside the verb phrase.
modifier_placement.example: The regulator, by then, had two versions of the same statement.
modifier_placement.effect: Slows the clause at the point of insertion and gives the adverbial a light stress.

modifier_placement.name: end-placed adverbial
modifier_placement.definition: An adverbial in final position, taking the sentence's end-focus.
