modifier_placement.example: She filed the complaint on the last day the statute allowed.
modifier_placement.effect: Puts the circumstance in the emphatic slot; the right choice when the circumstance is the news.

modifier_placement.name: split infinitive
modifier_placement.definition: An adverb placed between 'to' and the verb.
modifier_placement.example: The rule allowed the trustees to quietly reclassify anything held under a year.
modifier_placement.effect: Often the only placement that puts the adverb where its scope actually falls.
modifier_placement.caution: The prohibition is a nineteenth-century invention, but some readers still flinch; avoid splitting with a long phrase.

modifier_placement.name: adverb between auxiliary and verb
modifier_placement.definition: Placement of an adverb after the first auxiliary, the natural English position for many adverbs.
modifier_placement.example: The transfer had already been approved twice before anyone read the schedule.
modifier_placement.effect: The unmarked position; moving the adverb elsewhere is what creates emphasis.

modifier_placement.name: only-placement
modifier_placement.definition: The positioning of focusing adverbs — only, even, just, also — immediately before the constituent they restrict.
modifier_placement.example: 'He only signed two statements' and 'he signed only two statements' assert different things; the second is what is usually meant.
modifier_placement.effect: Placement is meaning, not fussiness; a misplaced 'only' misstates the claim.
modifier_placement.caution: In careful nonfiction, place focusing adverbs adjacent to their target even when speech would not.

modifier_placement.name: misplaced modifier
modifier_placement.definition: A modifier positioned so that it attaches to the wrong element.
modifier_placement.example: Faulty: 'She read the memo about the missing reserve in her car.' Repaired: 'In her car, she read the memo about the missing reserve.'
modifier_placement.effect: Named as a diagnostic: readers attach modifiers to the nearest plausible host, whatever the writer intended.
modifier_placement.caution: Prepositional-phrase pileups at the end of a clause are the usual site.

modifier_placement.name: stacked prenominal modifiers
modifier_placement.definition: Several modifiers accumulated before a noun.
modifier_placement.example: A three-page unsigned internal audit memo turned up in the file.
modifier_placement.effect: Compresses information into the noun phrase; standard in technical and bureaucratic writing.
modifier_placement.caution: Past three modifiers, readers cannot tell which modify the noun and which modify each other; unpack into a relative clause.

modifier_placement.name: prepositional-phrase chain
modifier_placement.definition: A sequence of prepositional phrases attached one after another at the end of a clause.
modifier_placement.example: The box was found in a closet on the second floor of an annex behind the courthouse.
modifier_placement.effect: Reads as a narrowing zoom when intended; as bureaucratic sludge when not.
modifier_placement.caution: Three or more attached to one verb is the most common cause of unreadable expository sentences.

modifier_placement.name: postposed modifier
modifier_placement.definition: A modifier moved from before the noun to after it, usually to relieve a heavy noun phrase.
modifier_placement.example: The pages missing from the binder were the ones dated in March.
modifier_placement.effect: Gets the head noun to the reader sooner, then modifies.

modifier_placement.name: sentence adverb
modifier_placement.definition: An adverb modifying the whole clause rather than any element in it: obviously, arguably, mercifully.
modifier_placement.example: Arguably, the reclassification was legal on the day it was made.
modifier_placement.effect: Encodes the writer's stance in one word; the cheapest available hedge or booster.
modifier_placement.caution: 'Obviously', 'clearly', and 'of course' most often mark claims the writer has not supported.

modifier_placement.name: adverbial of degree placement
modifier_placement.definition: The position of degree adverbs — quite, rather, almost, barely — relative to what they scale.
modifier_placement.example: 'The number was almost right' and 'almost the number was right' are not both available; degree adverbs sit tight against their target.
modifier_placement.effect: Governs whether the scaling applies to a word, a phrase, or the whole assertion.
modifier_placement.caution: Degree adverbs stacked on a strong verb usually weaken it; cut before repositioning.

sentence_length_moves.name: one-word sentence
sentence_length_moves.definition: A sentence consisting of a single word, usually after a long one.
sentence_length_moves.example: The bank spent nine months preparing a defense, hired three firms, and rehearsed the testimony twice. Nothing.
sentence_length_moves.effect: Maximum stress on one word; the syntactic equivalent of a full stop in speech.
sentence_length_moves.caution: Its power is entirely contrast; used twice on a page it is worth nothing.

sentence_length_moves.name: telegraphic sentence
sentence_length_moves.definition: A very short sentence, typically under six words, stripped of modifiers.
sentence_length_moves.effect: Reads as fact rather than interpretation; lands hardest after a sentence that has been building.

sentence_length_moves.name: minor sentence
sentence_length_moves.definition: A grammatically incomplete unit punctuated as a sentence — no finite verb, or no subject.
sentence_length_moves.example: Two boxes of paper. Nine days of testimony. One question at the end.
sentence_length_moves.effect: Isolates an element for stress and mimics the way attention actually lands on things.
sentence_length_moves.caution: The single most overused device in contemporary nonfiction; keep a count per chapter.

sentence_length_moves.name: long-breath sentence
sentence_length_moves.definition: A sentence extending across many clauses without breaking, usually held together by coordination or accumulating modifiers.
sentence_length_moves.example: They kept the plant on the letterhead and the sign on the road and the picture in the annual report, long after the last shift had gone and the parking lot had cracked and the town had stopped saying the name out loud.
sentence_length_moves.effect: Enacts duration or accumulation; the reader feels the length as time.
sentence_length_moves.caution: One per chapter, and it must be readable aloud in a single arc.

sentence_length_moves.name: labyrinthine sentence
sentence_length_moves.definition: A long sentence complicated by embedding and qualification rather than by coordination.
sentence_length_moves.example: The memo, which had been drafted by a deputy who reported to the officer whose signature appeared, though nobody could establish when, on the March statement, was never logged.
sentence_length_moves.effect: Renders complexity, bureaucracy, or an overloaded mind; the difficulty is the content.
sentence_length_moves.caution: Only works when the surrounding prose is clean enough that the difficulty reads as deliberate.

sentence_length_moves.name: short after long
sentence_length_moves.definition: Placing a very short sentence directly after a long one.
sentence_length_moves.example: For three years the committee requested the underlying schedules, first informally, then in writing, then through counsel, and each time received a summary instead. Nobody escalated.
sentence_length_moves.effect: The standard rhythm move of English prose: build, then land.

sentence_length_moves.name: long after short
sentence_length_moves.definition: Placing an expansive sentence directly after a clipped one, opening the field back up.
sentence_length_moves.example: The vote was unanimous. It was also, as the minutes would eventually show, taken without the schedule that three members had asked for twice and one had asked for in writing.
sentence_length_moves.effect: Releases the pressure a short sentence creates; the reader exhales into the long one.

sentence_length_moves.name: sentence-length alternation
sentence_length_moves.definition: Deliberate variation of sentence length across a passage rather than a uniform average.
sentence_length_moves.example: A paragraph of 8, 31, 12, 6, and 44 words reads as written; five sentences of 20 words each reads as generated.
sentence_length_moves.effect: Variance — not average length — is what makes prose sound like a person; low variance is the most reliable machine tell.

sentence_length_moves.name: run-on for effect
sentence_length_moves.definition: A deliberately fused sentence, clauses running together without the punctuation that would separate them.
sentence_length_moves.example: She read it again and then again and then she put it in the drawer and went out and did not come back until the building had emptied.
sentence_length_moves.effect: Renders panic, momentum, or a mind refusing to stop; the missing punctuation is the content.
sentence_length_moves.caution: Requires visibly controlled punctuation elsewhere or it reads as carelessness.

sentence_length_moves.name: single-sentence paragraph
sentence_length_moves.definition: A paragraph consisting of one sentence, set off by white space.
sentence_length_moves.effect: Borrows emphasis from layout rather than syntax; the eye stops before the mind does.
sentence_length_moves.caution: Overused in web-native prose to the point of parody; reserve for genuine turns.

sentence_length_moves.name: staccato series
sentence_length_moves.definition: Three or more short sentences in a row, each self-contained.
sentence_length_moves.example: The auditor called. The line was busy. She drove over. The office was dark.
sentence_length_moves.effect: Speeds narration and withholds interpretation; each fact lands separately.
sentence_length_moves.caution: Sustained past four or five, it flattens into a list of events.

sentence_length_moves.name: expanding series
sentence_length_moves.definition: Successive sentences of increasing length across a passage.
sentence_length_moves.example: It started small. Two accounts, then five, then a whole class of them. By the end of the year it covered every deposit the branch had taken in since the merger, and no one had written a memo about any of it.
sentence_length_moves.effect: Enacts growth or escalation in the shape of the prose itself.
sentence_length_moves.caution: Works only when the content escalates too; otherwise it is a pattern the reader notices and resents.

sentence_length_moves.name: contracting series
sentence_length_moves.definition: Successive sentences of decreasing length, narrowing toward a close.
sentence_length_moves.example: They had the documents, the dates, the signatures, and two people willing to testify about all of it. They had a year. They had nothing.
sentence_length_moves.effect: Produces a sense of closing in; the standard shape for the end of a section.
sentence_length_moves.caution: The last sentence carries everything, so it must be worth the shape.
